lessons.title: Nutrition across the life span

objectives: Describe nutritional needs in pregnancy, lactation, infancy and childhood
Describe the needs of adolescents, adults and older people
Describe common nutrition problems at each stage
reviewNotes: Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.
Life-span guidance follows WHO general recommendations; a nutritionist or midwife must review before release.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Pregnancy and lactation
blocks.md: Extra energy and nutrients are needed for the growth of the fetus and for milk production; particular attention to **iron**, **folate**, **iodine**, **calcium**, **vitamin A** and protein. Folate before and early in pregnancy helps prevent neural tube defects. Alcohol and smoking are avoided. Care in a health facility, including supplements where advised, is part of antenatal care.

blocks.title: Infancy
blocks.md: **Exclusive breastfeeding** for about the first six months (WHO) provides nutrients and protects against infection; complementary foods are added from about six months with continued breastfeeding up to two years or beyond. Complementary foods should be energy-dense, nutrient-rich (include animal foods or legumes, vegetables, fruit, a little oil), safe and prepared hygienically, given frequently. Common problems: stunting, anaemia, diarrhoea, overweight in some settings.

items.text: Life stage and key nutrition focus

blocks.caption: A table of four life stages with key nutrition focus.
blocks.alt: Table: pregnancy iron, folate and iodine; infancy breast milk and safe foods; adolescence iron and calcium; older age protein, calcium and fluids.

blocks.title: Childhood and adolescence
blocks.md: Children need nutrient-dense foods in small, frequent meals; school meals help. Adolescence has a **growth spurt**: higher needs for energy, protein, iron (especially girls), calcium and zinc. Risks: skipping meals, sugary drinks and snacks, body-image problems, early pregnancy, underweight and overweight.

blocks.title: Adults and older people
blocks.md: Adult needs depend on activity and health; focus on balance, fibre, fruit and vegetables, limiting salt, sugar and saturated fat, and physical activity. Older people need fewer calories but similar or higher protein, calcium, vitamin D, B12 and fluid; problems: poor appetite, chewing difficulties, loneliness, medicines, osteoporosis. Needs are individual; a health professional gives personal advice.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- 'Eating for two' does not mean doubling food; extra needs are moderate.
- Cereal-based thin porridges are often too low in energy and protein for infants.
- Do not give supplements without advice.
- Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Infant feeding
blocks.statement: Design a day's complementary feeds for a 9-month-old (general guidance).
steps: Continue breastfeeding on demand and offer 3 to 4 small meals of soft foods such as enriched pap with groundnut paste or egg, mashed plantain with fish, and fruit.
Prepare food fresh and hygienically; see the clinic for individual advice.
blocks.answer: Breastfeeding plus 3 to 4 enriched soft meals

blocks.title: Example 2 - Older adult
blocks.statement: An older woman eats little and has weak bones. Suggest general advice.
steps: Offer small frequent meals with protein foods (beans, fish, eggs) and calcium sources (small fish, milk, leaves).
Encourage safe sunlight, fluids and see a health worker for assessment.
blocks.answer: Small frequent meals, protein, calcium, medical check

objectives: Describe interventions: fortification, supplementation, education, breastfeeding promotion
Describe food security and its dimensions
Describe nutrition surveys and the first 1000 days
reviewNotes: Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.
Fortification examples are generic (country policies vary); the survey percentage is illustrative; Cameroon-specific data/programmes are not cited and should be added after review.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Indicators
blocks.md: **Stunting**: low height-for-age (chronic undernutrition). **Wasting**: low weight-for-height (acute). **Underweight**: low weight-for-age. **MUAC** (mid-upper arm circumference) is a quick screening tool for acute malnutrition. **Overweight** is also measured (BMI-for-age in children). Micronutrient deficiencies (iron, vitamin A, iodine, zinc) are often called 'hidden hunger'. The double burden: undernutrition and overweight in the same country or even family.

blocks.title: Interventions
blocks.md: **Food fortification** (adding micronutrients to common foods; examples in many countries include iodised salt and vitamin-enriched oil or flour), **supplementation** (e.g. iron-folic acid in pregnancy, vitamin A for young children where recommended), **nutrition education**, **promotion of breastfeeding**, **school feeding**, **sanitation and clean water**, **treatment of acute malnutrition**, and **biofortified crops**. The **first 1000 days** (pregnancy to age two) are a critical period.

blocks.caption: A table of four anthropometric indicators and what each shows.
blocks.alt: Table: height-for-age shows stunting, weight-for-height wasting, weight-for-age underweight, MUAC acute risk.

blocks.title: Food security
blocks.md: FAO describes four dimensions: **availability** (enough food produced or imported), **access** (people can afford or obtain it), **utilisation** (good use: nutrition, safe water, health) and **stability** (reliable over time). Threats: poverty, conflict, climate change, post-harvest losses, poor roads, price shocks.

blocks.title: Surveys
blocks.md: A **nutrition survey** may measure anthropometry (weight, height, MUAC), diet (24-hour recall, food frequency), clinical signs and biochemical tests; sampling must represent the population; results guide programmes. Ethical practice: consent, privacy and referral of children found to be malnourished.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Wasting and stunting are different: wasting is acute, stunting chronic.
- Fortification does not replace dietary variety.
- Food security is more than food production.
- Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Classify
blocks.statement: A child of normal weight is much shorter than expected for age. Which indicator is low and what does it show?

blocks.title: Example 2 - Intervention
blocks.statement: Suggest two community interventions to improve nutrition in a rural district.
steps: Nutrition education and promotion of breastfeeding and varied local foods.

objectives: Calculate moisture, protein (Kjeldahl factor), fat and carbohydrate by difference
Explain food composition tables and limitations
reviewNotes: Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.
All sample numbers are invented for practice. Oven temperatures and methods follow common AOAC-type practice in outline; check the practical guide.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Proximate analysis
blocks.md: Proximate analysis gives the main components: **moisture** (loss of mass on drying in an oven, e.g. at about 105 degrees Celsius to constant mass), **ash** (inorganic residue after burning in a furnace), **protein** (Kjeldahl: total nitrogen x **6.25**), **fat** (extraction with a solvent) and **crude fibre**. **Carbohydrate** is usually calculated **by difference**: 100 minus moisture, ash, protein and fat (all in g per 100 g).

blocks.title: Calculations
blocks.md: Moisture % = (mass lost / initial mass) x 100. Protein % = nitrogen % x 6.25 (6.25 assumes proteins are about 16% nitrogen). Carbohydrate (by difference) includes fibre unless fibre is measured separately. Energy per 100 g = 17 x carbohydrate + 17 x protein + 37 x fat (kJ), using the course values.

items.text: Illustrative composition of 100 g of a flour

blocks.caption: A stacked bar of an illustrative flour: moisture 15, ash 3, protein 20, fat 5 and carbohydrate 57 percent.
blocks.alt: Stacked bar of composition: moisture 15, ash 3, protein 20, fat 5, carbohydrate 57 percent.

blocks.title: Composition tables
blocks.md: Food composition tables give nutrients per 100 g of edible portion. Real values vary with variety, soil, season, processing and cooking. Raw and cooked values differ; use the **edible portion** (not the weight with peel and bones). Tables are for planning, not exact measurement of one meal.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using wet mass when dry mass is required.
- Forgetting the 6.25 factor (some foods use other factors).
- Treating table values as exact.
- Mixing 100 g raw values with cooked quantities.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Moisture
blocks.statement: A 5.00 g sample is dried and its mass falls to 4.25 g. Find the moisture content.

blocks.title: Example 2 - Energy
blocks.statement: 100 g of a flour: moisture 15 g, ash 3 g, protein 20 g, fat 5 g. Find carbohydrate by difference and energy.

lessons.title: Diet and non-communicable disease; food policy
lessons.programRef: Cameroon GCE Board — Advanced Level Food Science and Nutrition syllabus (Upper Sixth part) — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the link between diet and obesity, diabetes, hypertension and heart disease (outline)
Describe food labelling, advertising and policy tools
Evaluate a population diet in outline
reviewNotes: Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.
Disease associations are general; no numeric thresholds or Cameroonian prevalence statistics are given (to be added by a public-health reviewer).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Diet-related conditions
blocks.md: **Overweight and obesity**: energy intake above expenditure. **Type 2 diabetes**: raised blood glucose, associated with excess weight, inactivity and diet. **Hypertension** (high blood pressure): linked to high salt intake, excess weight and inactivity. **Cardiovascular disease**: linked to saturated and trans fats, smoking, high blood pressure and inactivity. **Dental decay** is linked to frequent sugary foods. These are **non-communicable diseases (NCDs)**; many share risk factors and are increasing in many African countries as diets and lifestyles change.

blocks.title: Prevention (general)
blocks.md: Maintain a healthy weight; be active; eat plenty of vegetables, fruit, legumes and whole grains; limit free sugars, saturated and trans fats and salt; use unsaturated oils in moderation; avoid tobacco and harmful use of alcohol. Specific values (for example daily salt or sugar limits) come from national and WHO guidelines and are not stated here.

blocks.caption: A table of four risk factors and the conditions linked to them.
blocks.alt: Table of risk factors: excess energy with obesity and diabetes, high salt with hypertension, saturated fat with heart disease, frequent sugar with dental decay.

blocks.title: Food policy
blocks.md: Governments and organisations use **food labelling** (nutrition information, allergen declaration, warnings), controls on **marketing to children**, **standards for fortification**, **food safety law and inspection**, **school food rules**, **taxes or subsidies**, and consumer education. The **Codex Alimentarius** is the international set of food standards agreed by member countries.

blocks.title: Evaluating a diet
blocks.md: Compare the food groups eaten with recommendations; check energy balance, variety, fibre, fat quality, sugar and salt; consider cost and access; suggest realistic changes (for example swapping sugary drinks for water, adding vegetables and legumes) and refer people with disease to health services for personal advice.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Diet alone does not cause NCDs; genes, activity, smoking and age also matter.
- Do not give personal medical advice; refer to health workers.
- 'Traditional' does not automatically mean healthy or unhealthy; look at the whole diet.
- Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Advice (general)
blocks.statement: A village health talk asks for general advice to reduce blood-pressure risk. State three general measures.
steps: Reduce added salt and salty processed foods, and keep a healthy weight.
Be physically active and eat more vegetables and fruit; people with high blood pressure should see a health worker.
blocks.answer: Less salt, healthy weight, activity, vegetables and fruit

blocks.title: Example 2 - Policy
blocks.statement: Name two policy tools that could reduce sugary-drink consumption by children.
steps: Restricting advertising aimed at children and limiting sales in schools.
Clear labelling and taxes or price measures where adopted.
blocks.answer: Marketing limits; school rules; labelling or taxes
